Function entry points and call sequences for installing or querying state are not shown.
Error codes and failure handling for control operations are not shown.
Timing guarantees and interrupt delivery ordering are not shown.
Memory ownership and lifetime for variable length attributes are not shown.
Validation rules for calendar fields and address payloads are not shown.

findings.text: The real time clock control interface provides paired enable and disable operations for four interrupt sources. One pair governs alarm delivery, a second governs periodic update delivery, a third governs periodic frequency delivery, and a fourth governs watchdog delivery.

The clock exposes operations to install and query a plain alarm moment, to fetch and adjust the current wall time, and to fetch and adjust both the periodic interrupt rate and the epoch value used when interpreting the hardware counter. Time and alarm exchanges use a calendar structure while rate and epoch exchanges use a wide unsigned integer.

Additional clock operations manage a wakeup alarm object with separate install and query directions, retrieve and install phase locked loop correction data, exchange generic driver parameters in both directions, and provide voltage condition retrieval plus a clear operation for latched low voltage state.

Five low voltage conditions are encoded as distinct single bit positions starting at the least significant bit. They distinguish invalid retained data from low backup supply, from missing or depleted backup, from degraded accuracy under low supply, and from a backup source change event.

Interrupt status is reported as a small bit set where one high bit indicates any source active, and three lower bits separately identify periodic activity, alarm expiry, and one hertz update activity.

Device capabilities are numbered from zero through seven with a count of eight marking the end. The positions cover plain alarm support, minute granularity, weekday requirement, two second granularity, update interrupt support, correction support, backup switch mode support, and wakeup only alarm behavior.

Generic parameter identifiers use zero for capability bits, one for correction, and two for backup switch mode. Backup behavior selects among disabled, direct, level triggered, and standby encodings zero through three. The highest periodic frequency supported is eight thousand one hundred ninety two hertz.
Two multicast routing protocol families occupy high family numbers for internet protocol version four and version six, with the family maximum equal to the larger of the two.

Routing netlink message identifiers begin at sixteen and advance in small groups per object family, typically covering creation, removal, retrieval, and sometimes mutation or notification variants. Derived quantities express the total identifier span, the number of four wide families, and a shift based mapping from identifier to family index.

The routing message family addresses link state, network addresses, forwarding entries, neighbor entries, policy rules, queueing disciplines, traffic classes, packet filters, packet actions, address prefixes, multicast and anycast membership, neighbor tables, discovery options, address labels, bridging controls, network configuration, multicast databases, namespace identifiers, statistics, cache reports, chains, nexthops and nexthop buckets, link properties, virtual local area network membership, and tunnel objects, each with creation removal and query variants where meaningful.
The generic routing attribute header consists of two sixteen bit unsigned fields, first a total length including header plus payload and second a type discriminator, followed by payload bytes.

Attributes use a four byte alignment boundary. Validity requires remaining length to hold a header and requires the embedded length to be at least header size and no larger than remaining length. Iteration advances by the aligned embedded length and reduces the remaining count accordingly. Length helpers add aligned header size to payload length or align that sum, while data access skips the aligned header and payload size subtracts it.

The route message header carries four single byte address qualifiers for family and destination length and source length and type of service, then four single byte route qualifiers for table and protocol and scope and type, followed by a wide unsigned flag word.

Route kinds distinguish unspecified, unicast, local reception, broadcast, anycast, multicast, blackhole discard, unreachable, prohibited, throw to another table, address translation, and external resolution, with a maximum marking the last valid kind.
Low numbered route installers identify unspecified, redirect originated, kernel originated, boot time, and administrator configured sources using values zero through four.

Higher installer numbers recognize many routing daemons and protocols, including gated and router advertisements and merit and zebra and bird and decnet daemon and xorp and netsukuku and dhcp client and multicast daemon and keepalived at eight through eighteen, plus babel, open virtual networking, open routing, border gateway, intermediate system, open shortest path, routing information, and enhanced interior gateway at scattered larger values.

Forwarding scope uses zero for universe with site, link, host, and nowhere at two hundred and two fifty three through two fifty five. Table selection uses zero for unspecified, plus compatibility, default, main, and local at two fifty two through two fifty five, with an all ones maximum.

Route flags request user notification, mark cloned and equalized multipath and prefix entries, request table lookup result return and full match return, and report hardware offload, trapping, and offload failure, with the failure bit placed high to avoid collision with version six route definitions.

Route attributes enumerate destination, source, input and output interface, gateway, priority, preferred source, metrics, multipath, flow, cache information, table, mark, multicast statistics, via, new destination, preference, encapsulation type and data, expiry, padding, user identifier, time to live propagation, protocol, source and destination ports, nexthop identifier, flow label, and deletion reason, bounded by a maximum. Helpers locate the first attribute after an aligned message header and compute remaining payload length.
Route removal causes distinguish unspecified, expiry driven garbage collection, and withdrawal by zero lifetime advertisement, with a maximum marking the end.
Each nexthop entry carries a sixteen bit total length, two single byte values for flags and hop count, and a signed integer output interface index, followed by optional attributes.

Nexthop flags mark dead multipath members, recursive gateway lookup, forced on link gateways, offloaded entries, carrier down, unresolved multicast entries, and trapping entries. A compare mask selects only dead, link down, offload, and trap bits for equality decisions.

Nexthop entries use four byte alignment with validity requiring embedded length to cover a header and fit within remaining length. Iteration steps by aligned length, length helpers add aligned header size to payload or align the sum, and data access skips the header to reach trailing attributes.

A via address pairs an address family with a variable length byte string. Cache information stores client reference count, last use timestamp, expiry delta, error code, use count, plus peer identity and timestamps for age computation when peer information is present.

Route metrics enumerate lock bitmap, maximum transmission unit, window, round trip time and variance, slow start threshold, congestion window, advertised segment size, reordering, hop limit, initial congestion and receive windows, feature bits, minimum retransmit timeout, quick acknowledgment, congestion control algorithm name, and fast open cookie policy, bounded by a maximum. Feature bits enable explicit congestion notification, selective acknowledgment, timestamps, fragmentation handling, and microsecond timestamps, combined into a mask.

A legacy session descriptor carries a protocol byte with padding then a union selecting a port pair, an internet control message type code and identifier, or a security parameter index. Multicast forwarding statistics count packets, bytes, and wrong interface arrivals as three sixty four bit counters.

A generic query carries only an address family byte. Link information carries family, padding, device type, interface index, current flags, and a change mask. Prefix information carries family, padding, interface index, prefix type, length, flags, and trailing padding.
Prefix attributes distinguish unspecified, address, and cache information with a maximum. Cache timing stores preferred and valid lifetimes as two thirty two bit values.

Traffic control messages carry family, padding, interface index, handle, parent selector, and detailed info. A special all ones interface index redirects the parent field to hold a block index instead. Queueing attributes enumerate kind, options, statistics and extended statistics, rate, filter count, secondary statistics, stabilization table, padding, dump visibility, chain, hardware offload, ingress and egress block, dump flags, and extended warning, bounded by a maximum. Helpers locate attributes after the header and compute payload length, and a terse flag requests minimal identifying data plus statistics.

Neighbor discovery user options carry family, padding, total option length, interface index, internet control message type and code, and padding, followed by one or more discovery options. Associated attributes distinguish unspecified and source address with a maximum.

Netlink multicast groups use single bit masks for link, notification, neighbor, and traffic control events, separate bits for version four and version six address, multicast route, route, and rule or prefix or interface information events, plus decnet address and route bits and a high bit for version six prefix events.

Interrupt control follows a two state model per source where an enable operation activates delivery and a matching disable operation deactivates it, independently across alarm, update, periodic, and watchdog sources. Routing objects follow a create remove query mutate cycle where creation installs state, removal withdraws it, query retrieves it, and set or notification variants adjust or announce it.

Stale time may be consumed if low voltage flags are ignored, since one condition marks retained data invalid and others signal degraded accuracy or backup loss or switchover. Forwarding may silently differ from intent when offload failure, trapping, dead or link down nexthop markings, or terse dumps that omit detail are not handled.
The routing header is protected by a single inclusion guard macro that ensures one definition per translation unit.
